newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. said proceeding with China rights resolution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said proceeding with China rights resolution.

text.p: With the death of Deng Xiaoping, the United States does not expect any quick improvement in human rights in China and plans to proceed with a U.N. resolution faulting Beijing's record, a senior U.S. official said Sunday.

As U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright prepared to make her first visit to Beijing on Monday, the official said that, while the trip is important, they do not expect major progress on any of the issues to be discussed, including human rights, trade, Taiwan, Hong Kong and nuclear non-proliferation.
China is the last stop on Albright's nine-nation tour of European and Asian capitals. She met Japanese leaders in Tokyo on Sunday.

"The emphasis in China over the coming weeks and months is likely to be on continuity, on stability within the leadership, on building consensus within the leadership, in other words nothing risky," said the senior official, who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity.
"Our expectations should not be too high," he said.

Albright has said that, with a lack of progress on human rights in China, the United States would co-sponsor a resolution faulting Beijing's record at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva next month.
"Based on the current situation we expect to proceed with the resolution," the official said. Most European Union members shared the U.S view of the situation, he said.

Albright, interviewed on ABC Television's "This Week", said Chinese leaders "expect me to raise human rights as an issue and I will." But she did not say what she would do on the resolution, which in the past has greatly angered Beijing.

She did, however, refuse to describe China as an "evil empire" -- as former President Ronald Reagan said of the Soviet Union. She reiterated U.S. support for one China governed from Beijing and reaffirmed backing for a policy of allowing U.S. visas in only limited cases to Taiwanese officials.

The official briefing reporters acknowleded that similar past human rights resolutions "have not had any obvious or visible effect upon China's human rights performance." Rather, the resolution's value was to ensure China is held accountable to international principles, he said

After taking office in 1993, President Bill Clinton linked improvements in human rights to most favoured nation trade benefits for China. But he later reversed that policy, arguing that engagment was the best way to encourage change.

The official said that, in Beijing, Albright would also "indicate that the United States has substantial interests in Hong Kong and we expect to see them protected" when the British colony is returned to China in July.
Albright would also make clear that Washington expected a series of high-level bilateral meetings planned for this year to produce concrete progress and not just symbolism, he said.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen is expected to visit Washington soon and U.S. Vice President Al Gore is due to go to Beijing thereafter, probably March.
Later, there is to be an exchange of summits in Beijing and Washington involving Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
